before.descent_text: Liberty Ridge is never descended — its loose rock, sustained steep ice, and total lack of rappel anchors or safe bivy terrain below Thumb Rock make down-climbing the ridge far more dangerous than continuing up and over the mountain; the NPS route brief is explicit that 'up was down' (ascending feels safer than retreating) is the dominant, and dangerous, pattern in the route's accident history. From the summit area, the standard descent drops off Liberty Cap's east side about 600 ft to Liberty Saddle, joins the Emmons-Winthrop route, and descends the broad Emmons Glacier via 'the Corridor' to Camp Schurman — NPS time estimates put this leg at just under three hours for an average party. From Camp Schurman, parties reverse the Emmons approach: around the south side of Steamboat Prow to Camp Curtis, down the Inter Glacier, and out via Glacier Basin to White River Campground (roughly another 3+ hours). This is a glacier walk-down with no rappelling required in a typical season — the real hazards are crevasse navigation (the Emmons/Winthrop shift through the summer and aren't wanded; a current GPS track is considered essential, and multiple Liberty Ridge parties have needed SOS rescue after losing the route here in whiteout) and large cornices that form on the east side of Liberty Saddle. A minority of parties instead descend the Winthrop Glacier from Camp Schurman toward lower Curtis Ridge/Moraine Park if they've pre-arranged a shuttle, to avoid re-crossing the Inter Glacier, but the Emmons-to-White River line is standard. No rappels on the descent.

before.season: Mid-May through early August; the ice chute holds good climbable ice into summer but the approach and glacier conditions degrade fast after August 1 (NPS)
before.rappels: 1-3 rappels to descend the upper ice step; NPS recommends Zero-Thread ice anchors over V-threads (V-threads can melt out before a party returns)
before.descent_text: Descent is normally either back down the Kautz Glacier itself (the way you came) or a carryover down the Disappointment Cleaver route to Paradise. On the headwall's ice steps specifically, with 60m ropes two double-rope rappels plus some downclimbing are enough to get back down through the steepest sections to the base of the ice pitches — rappel anchors on the ice steps are typically ice (V-thread/zero-thread) anchors, the modern standard per NPS guidance, not fixed bolts — old ascent-placed threads should not be reused. Expect 1-3 rappels through the upper step and 1-2 more through the lower step. This is a snow/ice route with no permanent hardware. In marginal conditions, some parties place running belays or fix a line through the ice steps instead of full rappels, both for the descent and to assist less-experienced members. Below the headwall, the Kautz/Wilson Glacier descent back to the Turtle or out via Comet Falls involves standard roped glacier travel, not further rappelling.

sling_rack.note: verbatim from a direct trip report: 'a rope, a cam, a few nuts, three screws, and one piton' — deliberately minimalist for speed through icefall exposure

before.rope_note: A direct trip report's minimalist rack used one rope (consistent with a 60m alpine rope); the route requires rappels off ice cliffs (e.g. ~75ft) using doubled strands off a single rope, plus an extra sling used at one rappel anchor.

crowds.peakTraffic: Narrow, cold frozen windows in late spring, if attempted at all
crowds.estimatePerSeason: Extremely rare - some years see zero ascents given the extreme, well-documented objective hazard; among the least-climbed lines on the mountain. The park's annual mountaineering reports do count it: 8 climbers attempted the route across 2006-2011, 6 of them in 2011 alone, against 10,830 climbers on the mountain that year - so five of those six years saw essentially nobody.

sling_rack.note: three independent trip reports converge: 'a rock rack was essential'

itinerary.totalNote: A remote 4-5 day trip (~12,000 ft gain); the climbing itself from high camp is quick, but the long approach and weather buffer make this one of the longest routes on the mountain.

before.rope_note: Single 60m rope for glacier travel plus short rappels off the ridge crest; trip report recommends carrying extra cord to leave at rappel anchors in case existing tat looks bad.
before.approach: From White River Campground (reached via WA-410 and White River Road — check nps.gov/mora road status for early/late-season openings), hike the Glacier Basin Trail roughly 3.5 miles and about 1,700 ft of gain to Glacier Basin (~5,900 ft), a broad basin with the last reliable running water and a common camping spot. From there, continue on climbers' path up to St. Elmo Pass (~7,400 ft), gaining another ~1,500 ft over roughly a mile of steepening scree/snow. At St. Elmo Pass, rope up for glacier travel: drop down onto the Winthrop Glacier and contour west/southwest, threading around crevasses, to reach the base of Curtis Ridge on its east (Winthrop) side. This is the same approach corridor used for Liberty Ridge, so expect other parties and established boot tracks in season. Above St. Elmo Pass there is no water; carry enough for the climb or plan to melt snow.

before.itinerary: Single-push day: drive to the Ruth Creek Road pullout near milepost 3 (2,950 ft); cross Ruth Creek and bushwhack to the base of Wall Street (~45 min); climb the snow couloir to the Northwest Glacier (~5,000 ft); cross the glacier to the 6,500-ft saddle; scramble the southeast ridge to the 7,191-ft summit (about 5.6 hours car-to-summit in one reported trip); descend the same line (about 2.8 hours back to the car).

before.overview: Named after the Neil Young song, Southern Man splits off from the Direct East Buttress about halfway up and climbs the south-facing headwall on SEWS's upper south side to the summit. First ascended by Mark Allen, Joel Kauffman, and Leaghan Falley, August 2008 (aided at 5.9+ C1); freed by B. Matthews and Bryan Burdo in 2010 at 5.11d (a September 2009 ascent by Burdo at 5.12a has also been reported but is unconfirmed — see data gaps).
